newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, Palestinians to study competitiveness.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Palestinians to study competitiveness.

text.p: Israel and the Palestinian Authority are undertaking a joint study aimed at identifying their national and regional competitive advantages, Israeli and Palestinian ministers said on Monday.
They will be joined by Egypt and Jordan in a project conducted under the aegis of Harvard University professor Michael Porter, a leading authority on competitive strategy.
"Political conflicts are not simple to resolve, but we are on the road," Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor said at a news conference to formally launch the project.

Nabil Shaath, the Palestinian planning and international cooperation minister, said ending Israel's closure of the borders between it and the West Bank and Gaza was an important first step in helping the Palestinian economy.

"There are environments that have to be created by the governments," he said after the new conference. "In my mind the single most important thing is to end the closure....Ending the closure puts mutuality and parity between the Palestinians and Israelis, and allows freedom of trade, which is the essence of Mr. Porter's ideas."

The study, which is being conducted by the Centre for Middle East Competitive Strategy and funded by the Dutch government, is being conducted by four national teams, supported by an international team. The study got underway last October.
The centre's work follows the ideas outlined by Porter's 1990 book: "The Competitive Advantage of Nations".

In the first phase, due to be completed at the end of March, the teams will establish benchmark assessments of each of the four countries' business environments. In particular, they will be identifying existing and potential groups of internationally competitive related industries.
In subsequent phases the teams will develop national action plans and recommendations on regional cooperation.
Porter said he believed that a regional strategy could lift the Middle East out of its economic doldrums.
"When you have a common framework for the region, all countries can move forward," he said, especially by developing regional trade.
"The Middle East is very unusual," he said. "In most parts of the world most trade is between neighbouring countries."

Porter said Israel's economy had been distorted by its history. The state of war it had been in with its Arab neighbours for most of its history had geared its trade towards Europe and the United States rather than the Middle East.
"Here because of the history, there is a chance to make a quantum leap," he said.
